column2: The statement {{c1::CREATE TRIGGER}} defines a trigger and names its triggering events.
column3:
The definition names the events and the body that runs when they occur. The application does not explicitly invoke that body.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditOrderInsert
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER INSERT
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.OrderAudit (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM inserted;
END;
Review source

column2: Triggers that respond to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements are {{c1::DML triggers}}.
column3:
DML triggers act on data changes rather than changes to table definitions. Fabric SQL database supports them, but Fabric Warehouse does not.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditOrderInsert
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER INSERT
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.OrderAudit (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM inserted;
END;
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column2: Triggers that respond to schema events such as CREATE, ALTER, or DROP are {{c1::DDL triggers}}.
column3:
DDL triggers act on definition changes rather than row changes. On Azure SQL Database and Fabric SQL database, use database scope.
CREATE TRIGGER AuditTableChanges
ON DATABASE
AFTER CREATE_TABLE, ALTER_TABLE, DROP_TABLE
AS
BEGIN
    PRINT 'A table definition changed.';
END;
Review source

column2: Use {{c1::AFTER INSERT}} to run trigger logic once an INSERT's actions and constraint checks succeed.
column3:
AFTER INSERT runs after the statement and constraint checks succeed, but before the surrounding transaction finishes. It does not run after commit.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditOrderInsert
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER INSERT
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.OrderAudit (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM inserted;
END;
Review source

column2: To implement replacement UPDATE logic for a view, define an {{c1::INSTEAD OF UPDATE}} trigger.
column3:
The trigger handles the view update in place of its ordinary write path. Its body can direct values to the appropriate base tables.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.UpdateCustomerName
ON dbo.CustomerNames
INSTEAD OF UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    UPDATE c SET CustomerName = i.CustomerName
    FROM dbo.Customers AS c
    JOIN inserted AS i ON i.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;
END;
Review source

column2: Inside an AFTER INSERT trigger, read new OrderID values with SELECT OrderID FROM {{c1::inserted}};
column3:
inserted is the statement's set of new rows. Read it as a rowset so the logic works when a statement inserts several orders.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditOrderInsert
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER INSERT
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.OrderAudit (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM inserted;
END;
Review source

column2: Inside an AFTER DELETE trigger, read removed OrderID values with SELECT OrderID FROM {{c1::deleted}};
column3:
deleted contains the removed versions even though the base table no longer returns them. It can supply values for a deletion audit.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditOrderDelete
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER DELETE
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.OrderAudit (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM deleted;
END;
Review source

column2: An UPDATE trigger sees old rows in deleted and new rows in {{c1::inserted}}.
column3:
Compare the two rowsets to find changed values. Match rows by an unchanged key rather than assuming either rowset has a reliable order.
-- SQL Server 2022 or later.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditPriceUpdate
ON dbo.Products
AFTER UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.PriceAudit (ProductID, OldPrice, NewPrice)
    SELECT i.ProductID, d.Price, i.Price
    FROM inserted AS i
    JOIN deleted AS d ON d.ProductID = i.ProductID
    WHERE d.Price IS DISTINCT FROM i.Price;
END;
Review source

column2: One INSERT statement adding 100 rows directly invokes each matching INSERT trigger {{c1::once}}.
column3:
The single invocation sees all 100 new rows in inserted. Do not write the body as though each call receives one row.
Review source

column2: A SQL Server DML trigger that can receive several affected rows should use {{c1::set-based logic}} rather than process one arbitrary row.
column3:
For example, aggregate order quantities by ProductID in one query. A set-based update can then apply the totals without a cursor.
Review source

column2: Compute total ordered quantity per product with SELECT ProductID, {{c1::SUM(Quantity)}} AS TotalQuantity FROM inserted GROUP BY ProductID;
column3:
Grouping makes one summary row for each product. The inventory update can subtract each product's full quantity rather than choosing an arbitrary order line.
SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) AS TotalQuantity
FROM inserted
GROUP BY ProductID;
Review source

column2: UPDATE(Price) identifies {{c1::an attempt to write Price}}, not proof that its value changed.
column3:
The test tells you what the write targeted. To log real changes, compare deleted.Price with inserted.Price and handle NULL explicitly.
IF UPDATE(Price)
BEGIN
    -- This detects an attempted assignment, not a value change.
    PRINT 'Price was targeted';
END;
Review source

column2: Detect nullable old/new price differences in SQL Server 2022 and later with oldPrice {{c1::IS DISTINCT FROM}} newPrice.
column3:
This predicate distinguishes a missing price from a known price. It also treats two NULL prices as not distinct.
-- SQL Server 2022 or later.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditPriceUpdate
ON dbo.Products
AFTER UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.PriceAudit (ProductID, OldPrice, NewPrice)
    SELECT i.ProductID, d.Price, i.Price
    FROM inserted AS i
    JOIN deleted AS d ON d.ProductID = i.ProductID
    WHERE d.Price IS DISTINCT FROM i.Price;
END;
Review source

column2: A trigger can cover all three row-modification events with {{c1::AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE}}.
column3:
The comma-delimited list attaches one trigger to all three operations. Its body still needs to account for the different contents of inserted and deleted.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.TrackOrderChange
ON dbo.Orders
AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    -- Process inserted and deleted as sets.
END;
Review source

column2: Pair old and new UPDATE rows by joining inserted and deleted on an {{c1::unchanged, non-NULL unique key}}.
column3:
A stable key ties each old version to its new version in any row order. A value that changes during the update is not a reliable match key.
-- SQL Server 2022 or later.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.AuditPriceUpdate
ON dbo.Products
AFTER UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.PriceAudit (ProductID, OldPrice, NewPrice)
    SELECT i.ProductID, d.Price, i.Price
    FROM inserted AS i
    JOIN deleted AS d ON d.ProductID = i.ProductID
    WHERE d.Price IS DISTINCT FROM i.Price;
END;
Review source

column2: To defer expensive processing, write event details to a {{c1::queue table}} for a separate job.
column3:
The queue entry can commit with the row change. A separate worker can then process it without holding up the triggering request.
Review source

column2: A DML trigger and the statement that fires it participate in {{c1::the same transaction}}.
column3:
The trigger does not commit independently. A rollback of the original transaction can undo both the statement and changes made by the trigger.
Review source

column2: Raise a trigger validation error with {{c1::THROW}} 50001, 'Order date cannot be in the future', 1;
column3:
This form raises a user-defined error when the trigger finds an invalid row. SQL Server reports it as a failure, not as query result data.
IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inserted WHERE OrderDate > GETDATE())
    THROW 50001, 'Order date cannot be in the future.', 1;
Review source

column2: The database option {{c1::RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS}} controls direct recursion of AFTER triggers.
column3:
This option determines whether an AFTER trigger can directly fire itself. Indirect nesting is a separate behavior.
Review source

column2: RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS OFF blocks {{c1::direct recursion of AFTER triggers}}, not every trigger loop.
column3:
An A-to-B-to-A chain can still recur indirectly. Do not treat this setting as a complete safeguard against trigger cycles.
Review source

column2: To skip trigger work when the firing statement affects no rows, begin with IF {{c1::ROWCOUNT_BIG() = 0}} RETURN;.
column3:
Read the affected-row count as soon as the trigger starts. Later statements can change the count and make the test unreliable.
IF ROWCOUNT_BIG() = 0
    RETURN;
-- Process the inserted and deleted rowsets here.
